name: Mondunga
confidence_why: De Boeck's 1952 grammar and Bokula's 1982 comparative study, the only first-hand descriptions of Mondunga, both give it two fixed tones (high and low) and say nothing of word stress, and Tucker and Bryan's 1966 survey agrees on the two lexical tones while adding only a hedged, group-level remark that stress 'seems to fall' on the first syllable of the stem, so the tonal reading rests on few but concordant sources.

catalog_quote: 3. La tonologie: Le système tonologique ne possède que deux tons 'simples'; le ton haut et le ton bas. Il n'y a pas de ton moyen avec valeur tonologique. Les tons sont fixes: c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton.

new_statements.translation: 3. Tonology: The tonological system has only two 'simple' tones: the high tone and the low tone. There is no mid tone with tonological value. The tones are fixed: i.e. the syllables in words always have the same tone. Only in very rare and well-defined cases does a syllable change tone.

Les tons sont fixes : c.-à-d. que les syllables dans les mots ont toujours le même ton. Ce n'est que dans des cas très rares et bien déterminés qu'une syllable change de ton." Verbatim against the page scan, including the spelling "syllables/syllable"; only the apostrophe glyphs differ. Index (p. 4) confirms Ch. I Phonologie = 1. Les voyelles p. 7, 2. Les consonnes p. 7, 3. La tonolo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndunga is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexically fixed tone on every syllable; no word stress or accent is described or mentioned anywhere in the grammar. The independent second description (Bokula 1982, pp. 119-120) agrees: two simple tones, high and low, borne by vowels only, generally fixed, and likewise says nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress of any kind is mentioned).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone, not stress: rare well-defined tone changes; contour (falling, rising, 'triple') tones on final syllables arising from suffix contraction (pp. 14-16); low tone on nominal suffixes of isolated nouns in Ndunga (Bokula 1982 p. 121). De Boeck's only use of 'accent' is 'accent descendant', a falling-tone diacritic (~p. 38).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tones of syllables within words, citation forms of nouns/verbs). The statement is a tone statement; both first-hand sources are silent on stress rather than asserting its absence. Bokula 1982 p. 119 calls his tone remarks a preliminary sketch pending a full tonological study of the Mba group.
new_statements.identity_note: De Boeck 1952 describes 'Mondunga' of Lisala (Roby-Lisala, 1950 fieldwork) = Ndunga ndun1249 (ISO ndt); Bokula 1982 describes 'ndúngá' (locally 'mondunga'/'bondunga') spoken in eight villages on the Lisala-Businga and Modzamboli roads — the same variety. No dialects are distinguished in either source.

new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress. 2a. There appear to be only two tone levels lexically—High and Low; Mid tone and Falling tone occur grammatically. Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted. 2b. Stress, sometimes accompanied by a slight degree of length, seems to fall on the first syllable of a word Stem. The Noun Class Suffix is never stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog holds only De Boeck 1952's tone description (two tones, no stress statement). T&B 1966 agrees on two lexical tones and adds a tentative stress placement (stem-initial, class suffix never stressed). The statement is made for the Mba group as a whole (Mba, Ndunga, 'Dongo, Ma), with the Ndunga data drawn from De Boeck 1952 (who says nothing about stress) plus Hackett's field notes, so it is group-level rather than Ndunga-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two lexical tones (H, L) with grammatical Mid and Falling; stress, sometimes with slight lengthening, seems to fall on the first syllable of the word stem (i.e. stem-initial, not word-initial where a prefix precedes); the noun-class suffix is never stressed. Hedged ('seems to').
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the hedge 'seems to fall'; the noun-class suffix is explicitly excluded from stress.
new_statements.identity_note: T&B 1966 ch. 4 treats the four Mba-group languages together (Mba 'Kimanga', Ndunga 'Mondunga', 'Dongo, Ma 'Amadi'); its sec. 2 statement is not attributed to any one of them. T&B 1956 identifies Ndunga (Mondunga, Bondonga), own name ndunga-lé, eight villages in Territoire Lisala, c. 2,500 speakers, the same variety De Boeck 1952 describes.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. De Boeck 1952 (already in the catalog) describes two fixed tones and makes no stress statement; Bokula 1982 likewise gives only tone. Tucker & Bryan 1966 agree on two lexical tones and add a hedged, group-level claim that stress 'seems to fall on the first syllable of a word Stem' and never on the noun-class suffix. The tension is only one of coverage: the sole first-hand Ndunga grammar (De Boeck) is silent on stress, so the T&B placement rests on Hackett's field notes and on Carrington's Mba material generalised to the group; it should be recorded as a tentative group-level stress statement, not as a Ndunga-specific finding.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Ch. I 'Phonologie' (pp. 7-9): 7 vowels, no nasal vowels, vowel length mostly from contraction; §3 'La tonologie' p. 9: two tones only (high, low), no phonemic mid tone, tones fixed on syllables, rare determined tone changes. Later pages describe falling/rising/'triple' tones on final syllables from suffix contraction. The word 'accent' occurs only as 'accent descendant' = falling-tone diacritic (verb infix, ~p. 38). text good (ABBYY); p. 9 verified against page scan.
